mioc-122.title: The Pannonian Sea is cut off
mioc-122.text: The Paratethys did not vanish all at once. It broke into pieces. Around 10 Ma the Carpathian mountains rose, and their uplift isolated the Pannonian Sea from the rest of the Paratethys. Each such cut left a smaller, more isolated body of water behind, on its own path.

mioc-119.title: Baja California tears away from Mexico
mioc-119.text: Rifting began opening the Gulf of California 10–6 Ma, tearing the Baja California peninsula northwest from mainland Mexico. Geologists widely date the gulf itself to around 5.3 million years ago, when the rift tore Baja California off the North American plate. The East Pacific Rise, a mid-ocean spreading ridge, pushed up the middle of the gulf, forming the Gulf of California Rift Zone. The new gulf changed the rivers around it. Its opening around 6 Ma let a large river cut its way northeast. By 5.5–5 Ma, streams there had merged into one major river, the subject of {{ref:plio-010}}.

mioc-126.title: Oreodonts fade as deer and bovids arrive
mioc-126.text: North America's cast of mammals changed in the Hemphillian age, from about 9.4 Ma. Old residents bowed out. The last oreodonts, mylagaulids and dromomerycids died out. Newcomers walked in from Asia: deer, bovids, saber-toothed cats and skunks. At home, rabbits and short-faced bears diversified. Several animals now familiar in North America, from deer to skunks, first arrived on the continent in this turnover.

mioc-137.title: Humans and chimpanzees go separate ways
mioc-137.text: Your closest living relative is the chimpanzee, and the question of when the two lines parted has no settled answer. The order of branching is clear. Gibbons split off first, then orangutans, then gorillas, before the lines leading to chimpanzees and humans separated. Their last common ancestor was probably a small African ape. The date is the hard part. A 2026 meta-analysis found that genome-based estimates fitting the fossil record put the split at about 8 Ma, almost certainly more than 7 Ma. Other molecular estimates scatter widely: 10–13 Ma in 1998, 9.3–6.5 Ma in 2016, 6.6–4.7 Ma in 2022 and 6.3–5.5 Ma in 2025. Fossils pushed back on the youngest numbers. Hominins such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin did not fit older molecular dates of 6–4 Ma. The parting may not have been clean either. The two lineages may have kept exchanging genes as late as 6.3–5.4 Ma. Researchers still disagree, with estimates running from about 13 to 4.7 Ma.

mioc-142.title: The Banda Arc meets Australia
mioc-142.text: In the Messinian, the Banda Arc, a curved chain of volcanic islands, began colliding with Australia and Timor. Geologists use it as a standard example of how an island arc crashes into a continent and builds a mountain belt, an orogen, along the seam.

mioc-144.title: Sahelanthropus and the skull called Toumaï
mioc-144.text: A partial skull found in northern Chad, nicknamed Toumaï, is the main evidence for Sahelanthropus. It lived about 7 Ma, with averaged sample ages giving 7.2–6.8 Ma. It is often listed as the first hominin, and the human line of upright-walking apes has been traced back to it. Its place is disputed. Some of its anatomy has been proposed as matching the last common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans, and other researchers reject that reading.

mioc-143.title: The desmostylians die out
mioc-143.text: Desmostylians are the only known extinct order of marine mammals. Native to the North Pacific, they declined after the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum, perhaps because Late Miocene cooling was unusually severe. They died out for good between 7.2 and 5.3 Ma.

mioc-148.title: Thalassocnus, the sloth that swam
mioc-148.text: A ground sloth went to sea. The oldest fossils of Thalassocnus, adapted to marine life on South America's Pacific coast, date to roughly 7 Ma in Peru. It is now known from many Miocene–Pliocene rock units along the coast, including Chile's Coquimbo Formation.

mioc-145.title: C4 grasses take over the grasslands
mioc-145.text: Grass is tough to eat, and a new kind made it tougher. C4 grasses use carbon dioxide and water more efficiently than C3 grasses, the older type. Between 7 and 6 Ma they became ecologically significant, though not yet in the north. As carbon dioxide kept falling, C4 plants came to dominate grasslands over the last 10 million years. They changed who could eat. Silica-rich C4 grasses wore down teeth, and herbivores without high-crowned teeth went extinct worldwide. The cause of the spread is still argued over. Some point to falling carbon dioxide. Others point to rising seasonality and aridity, with wildfires fed by the monsoons. The shift was large enough to mark the whole planet. It left its imprint on the global carbon cycle, visible in carbon isotope records.

mioc-147.title: The sharp Late Miocene cooling
mioc-147.text: Between 7 and 5.3 Ma temperatures fell sharply, most likely from declining carbon dioxide and a smaller swing in Earth's axial tilt. Ocean temperatures dropped to near-modern values, with sea surfaces outside the tropics cooling by about 7–9 °C. Antarctic ice neared its present size. Significant glaciation from 6.26 to 5.50 Ma kept time with the 41,000-year tilt cycle, dominant since 7.7 Ma. A cold spell around 6 Ma advanced glaciers and lowered sea level, helping start the crisis in {{ref:mioc-154}}. Around then the carbon cycle reorganized too: carbon stores on land stopped growing during cold spells.

mioc-149.title: The first mammoth lives in Africa
mioc-149.text: Mammoths began not in the frozen north but in Africa. The oldest, Mammuthus subplanifrons, appeared in southern and eastern Africa around 6.2-5.3 million years ago. Mammoths went on to live in Africa, Asia, Europe and North America until about 4,000 years ago. A 2010 study suggests mammoths and Asian elephants split 7.8-5.8 million years ago, after the African elephant line had branched off 8.8-6.6 million years ago.

mioc-150.title: Orrorin, an early hominin that walked upright
mioc-150.text: In Kenya's Lukeino Formation, fossils of Orrorin tugenensis date from 6.1 to 5.7 Ma. Orrorin appears to have walked upright on two legs about 6 Ma. Its fossils share no derived features, the new traits that mark a lineage, with the great apes. It belongs instead with the early hominins. The rise of two-legged apes at the end of the Miocene sped up the turnover of Africa's animals.

mioc-151.title: Trachilos footprints: a puzzle on Crete
mioc-151.text: On western Crete, possible footprints with hominin-like features have been dated to about 6.05 Ma, older than an earlier 5.7 Ma estimate. If a hominin made them, they would predate other hominin footprints by about two million years. They may instead record an ape that evolved similar feet independently. Critics doubt they are footprints at all, and the claim clashes with the accepted African origin of hominins.

mioc-152.title: Argentavis, a giant of the South American skies
mioc-152.text: Argentavis had a wingspan of 6 m or more, making it one of the largest flying birds known. This teratorn soared over South America about 6 Ma. It may have fed partly on leftovers from the kills of Thylacosmilus, a saber-toothed predator.

mioc-153.title: The Nile carves the deep Eonile gorge
mioc-153.text: At Cairo, the ancestral Nile cut its bed 2,400 m below sea level. As the Mediterranean emptied, the river chased the falling shoreline and carved a deep gorge, the Eonile, through Egypt. At Aswan it reached several hundred metres below sea level. When the sea refilled, the gorge became a gulf that slowly filled with sediment.

mioc-154.title: The Messinian crisis: the Mediterranean dries out
mioc-154.text: Around 5.6 Ma, the Mediterranean Sea dried almost completely within a thousand years. It was the climax of the Messinian salinity crisis. From 5.96 to 5.33 Ma the sea dried out in cycles, sometimes partly and sometimes almost entirely, and evaporites piled up across its floor. The crisis began basin-wide at 5.96 ± 0.02 Ma. The Betic corridor and the precursor of the Strait of Gibraltar closed, sealing the sea off from the Atlantic. Several causes worked together: plate motion at the Gibraltar Arc, mountain uplift in the western Mediterranean, and glacial sea-level falls of about 10 m from about 6.14 Ma. With the sea gone, rivers cut canyons on the scale of the Grand Canyon, as {{ref:mioc-153}} shows. Native marine animals suffered major extinctions. From 5.5 Ma river water diluted the brines into brackish 'Lago Mare' lakes. Then, at 5.33 Ma, the Strait of Gibraltar reopened, in the flood told in {{ref:plio-009}}.

mioc-155.title: Cerro Guacha's supereruption
mioc-155.text: High in the Andes, about 5.65 Ma, Cerro Guacha erupted the Guacha ignimbrite, roughly 1,200–1,300 km³ of rock. It was one of the giant eruptions at the peak of the Altiplano–Puna flare-up described in {{ref:mioc-115}}, when the region's calderas were at their most violent.

mioc-156.title: Ardipithecus appears in East Africa
mioc-156.text: The genus Ardipithecus appeared around 5.5 Ma, probably after the human–chimpanzee split, though the two lines may still have been swapping genes. An early form, A. kadabba, joined Sahelanthropus and Orrorin among the first hominins in Africa at the very end of the Miocene. Its fossils from the Middle Awash date 6.5–5.5 Ma.

mioc-157.title: The Caspian Sea becomes landlocked
mioc-157.text: The Caspian Sea, some 30 million years old, lost its link to the open ocean about 5.5 Ma. Two forces closed the door. Tectonic uplift raised the land around it, and sea level fell. From then on the Caspian was landlocked, the state in which it survives today.

mioc-158.title: Pastos Grandes erupts the Chuhuilla ignimbrite
mioc-158.text: At 5.45 ± 0.02 Ma, Pastos Grandes caldera in the Andes erupted the Chuhuilla ignimbrite, about 1,200 km³ of rock. It was the caldera's first great collapse cycle. Pastos Grandes joined a crowd of Andean calderas then erupting on this scale in {{ref:mioc-115}}.

mioc-159.title: The Dead Sea Transform forms
mioc-159.text: Toward the end of the Miocene, the Arabian plate began colliding with Eurasia. A new boundary developed: the Dead Sea Transform, where the Arabian and African plates now slide past each other. Rifting in the Gulf of Suez, active since {{ref:olig-041}}, ceased.

mioc-160.title: Europe's apes disappear
mioc-160.text: About 100 ape species lived across Africa, Asia and Europe during the Miocene. It was the great age of apes. In Europe, that age ended with the epoch. Europe's apes died out at the end of the Miocene as habitats became more uniform. Apes such as Danuvius and Graecopithecus, met earlier in this chapter, belonged to that vanished European ape world.

mioc-161.title: The Khersonian crisis empties the megalake
mioc-161.text: Near the end of the Miocene, the Paratethys megalake went through the Khersonian crisis. Conditions and lake levels swung rapidly. The swings wiped out much of the lake's unique fish fauna, species found nowhere else.

mioc-162.title: The Miocene ends in warmth
mioc-162.text: The cold of the Messinian did not last. At the end of the Miocene, global temperatures rose again as the swing in Earth's axial tilt grew. Central Asia grew more arid. The Pliocene began warmer than the cool Messinian that came before it.

reviews.late-miocene: The Late Miocene was a world getting colder and drier. Cooling dried the air worldwide, and C4 grasses spread so widely that herbivores without high-crowned teeth went extinct. Seaways closed and basins dried: the Caspian became landlocked, the Paratethys shrank to a megalake, and the Mediterranean itself dried out in the Messinian salinity crisis. Through it all, in Africa, the human and chimpanzee lines parted, and early hominins such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin appeared.
